info.title: Assinafy API Reference
info.description:
The **Assinafy API** is RESTful and gives access to documents, users, workspaces and signers, authenticated with an API key or an access token. ## REST API HTTP verbs are used according to the request type: - `GET` to retrieve data; - `POST` to create; - `PUT` to update; - `DELETE` to remove. ### Content type The default request and response format is JSON. ### HTTPS and TLS All requests must use HTTPS with **TLS 1.2 or higher**. Connections using TLS 1.0 or 1.1 are rejected during the handshake, before any HTTP response is sent, so they fail with a connection error rather than an HTTP status code. If your client reports errors such as `unsupported protocol` or `Could not create SSL/TLS secure channel`, update its runtime or HTTP library, or enable TLS 1.2 explicitly (older Java and .NET Framework versions may need this). ### Response envelope Every response is wrapped as `{ status, message, data }`. `status` mirrors the HTTP status code (`200` means success); `data` holds the payload on success and is `null` on error. ### Authentication Most endpoints require authentication. There are two options: a fixed **API key** (`X-Api-Key` header) or an **access token** (`Authorization: Bearer ...`). See the Authentication section for details. Applications that act in *other people's* workspaces use OAuth instead — see **OAuth Integration Guide**. ## Searching, paginating and sorting List endpoints accept these query parameters: | Parameter | Description | |-----------|-------------| | `search` | Search term. | | `page` | Page number. | | `per-page`| Records per page (max 100). | | `sort` | Sort order, e.g. `name` or `-created_at`. | …and return pagination metadata in response headers: `X-Pagination-Current-Page`, `X-Pagination-Total-Count`, `X-Pagination-Page-Count`, `X-Pagination-Per-Page`. ## Test and production environments During development use the **sandbox**:
API: https://sandbox.assinafy.com.br/v1 · APP: https://app-sandbox.assinafy.com.br When ready, switch to **production**:
API: https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1 · APP: https://app.assinafy.com.br ## Error codes The error code is returned in the `status` attribute. | Code | Type | |------|------| | 400 | Bad Request | | 401 | Unauthorized | | 403 | Forbidden | | 404 | Not Found | | 415 | Unsupported Media Type | | 429 | Too Many Requests | | 500 | Internal Server Error | ## Client libraries and tools Official SDKs for eight languages, a CLI, an MCP server and an n8n node are listed under **SDKs & Tools**. To work from the spec directly — Postman, Insomnia or your own generated client — see **OpenAPI & API Clients**.

post.description:
Request signatures on a document. Use `method: virtual` to sign without input fields, or `method: collect` to place input fields on specific pages.

For **virtual**, the document may be in `uploaded`, `metadata_processing` or `metadata_ready`; it is promoted to `pending_signature` automatically once metadata processing completes. For **collect**, the document must be in `metadata_ready` (fields reference specific pages).

`step` controls signing order: signers sharing a step sign in parallel, and the next step is notified only after the previous step completes. If supplied, every signer must supply it and values must be contiguous starting at 1.

verification_method.description: How the signer's identity is verified before signing. `Email` (default) sends a one-time code to the signer's email; `Whatsapp` sends the code over WhatsApp — the verification itself is not billed, but it requires the WhatsApp notification channel, so the signer costs 0.45 credits (available only on paid subscriptions); `DigitalCertificate` has the signer sign with their own ICP-Brasil certificate (A1/A3) — it requires the Digital Certificate feature, the signer must have a CPF or CNPJ in `government_id`, must be alone in its signing step, and is charged 2 credits per signer. A CPF requires that person's certificate (an e-CPF, or an e-CNPJ naming them as legal representative); a CNPJ requires an e-CNPJ for that company, from any of its representatives. Omit to default to `Email`.

notification_methods.description: How the signer is told a signature is being requested. **Exactly one method per signer** — the array shape is historical, and sending two returns `400`. The method must also be compatible with `verification_method`: `Email` verification takes `Email`, `Whatsapp` verification takes `Whatsapp`, and `DigitalCertificate` takes either. WhatsApp incurs an additional cost and is available only on paid subscriptions. Omit it to have it inferred from `verification_method`, or `{"Email"}` when neither is sent. See **Verification & Notification Methods** for the full pairing table.

entries.description: Required for `collect`: field placements per page.

message.description: Text included in the invitation email.

expires_at.description: ISO 8601; default is no expiration. Must be at least one hour in the future.

copy_receivers.description: Signer IDs that only receive a copy.

post.description:
Estimate the cost of creating an assignment without creating it, returning a cost breakdown and the current account balances. Signer IDs are not required — only the verification/notification method affects cost. Each assignment consumes 1 document from the plan allowance; if exhausted, an extra document is charged from credits (`needs_extra_document` = true). `blocking_reason` may be `PendingPayment`, `InsufficientDocuments` or `InsufficientCredits`.

### Pricing

Per-unit costs (in credits) used to build the estimate:

| Item | Cost |
|------|------|
| Extra document | 1 credit |
| Email notification | 0 credits |
| WhatsApp notification | 0.45 credits |
| Digital certificate signature (per signer) | 2 credits |

Verification methods are not priced separately — every line in the `breakdown` is a notification or a signature. A `Whatsapp`-verified signer therefore shows up as a WhatsApp notification, because that channel is mandatory for that verification method. A `DigitalCertificate` signer adds the digital-certificate signature cost **on top of** its notification cost; it appears in the `breakdown` under the `SignatureDigitalCertificate` code.

[Copy as Markdown](https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/markdown?method=post&path=%2Fv1%2Fdocuments%2F%7BdocumentId%7D%2Fassignments%2Festimate-cost) [Open in ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/?q=Read%20the%20API%20documentation%20at%20https%3A%2F%2Fapi.assinafy.com.br%2Fv1%2Fdocs%2Fmarkdown%3Fmethod%3Dpost%26path%3D%252Fv1%252Fdocuments%252F%257BdocumentId%257D%252Fassignments%252Festimate-cost%20and%20help%20me%20integrate%20this%20endpoint.) post.summary: Exchange a code, refresh token, or subject token for an access token
post.description:
Implements the RFC 6749 §5.1/§5.2 token-endpoint body contract in
     *         both directions: a successful exchange returns a flat JSON object with
     *         `access_token` at the top level, and a failure returns a flat
     *         `{error, error_description}` object — neither is wrapped in this API's
     *         usual response envelope, since no standard OAuth client library (or MCP
     *         connector) would find `access_token` or `error` inside a `data` key.
     *
     *         The third grant, `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange` (RFC 8693),
     *         is restricted to a confidential internal-service client (see `/oauth/introspect`)
     *         and trades a front-end resource's access token (the `subject_token`) for one
     *         minted for THIS API — the crossing an MCP server makes after a user consents,
     *         since its own token can never be forwarded here directly. The issued token is
     *         never wider than the subject: `scope`, when sent, must be a subset of the
     *         subject's own scopes, and `resource` must equal this API's own resource
     *         identifier exactly. No refresh token is issued; the caller re-exchanges from
     *         the user's own token instead of holding unattended API access.

[Copy as Markdown](https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/markdown?method=post&path=%2Fv1%2Foauth%2Ftoken) [Open in ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/?q=Read%20the%20API%20documentation%20at%20https%3A%2F%2Fapi.assinafy.com.br%2Fv1%2Fdocs%2Fmarkdown%3Fmethod%3Dpost%26path%3D%252Fv1%252Foauth%252Ftoken%20and%20help%20me%20integrate%20this%20endpoint.) [Open in Claude](https://claude.ai/new?q=Read%20the%20API%20documentation%20at%20https%3A%2F%2Fapi.assinafy.com.br%2Fv1%2Fdocs%2Fmarkdown%3Fmethod%3Dpost%26path%3D%252Fv1%252Foauth%252Ftoken%20and%20help%20me%20integrate%20this%20endpoint.)

grant_type.description: `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange` is for internal service clients only (Assinafy's own MCP server) — an ordinary confidential or public client authenticates with it and always gets `invalid_client`, exactly as an unrecognized client would. Everyday integrators use `authorization_code` and `refresh_token`.

code_verifier.description: RFC 7636: 43-128 characters from [A-Za-z0-9-._~]. Shorter values are rejected with `invalid_grant`.

client_secret.description: Confidential clients only. Public clients authenticate with PKCE and are never issued a secret; the token-exchange grant requires a confidential, internal-service client and therefore always requires this.

resource.description: RFC 8707 resource indicator. For `authorization_code`/`refresh_token`, optional; when present it must be the `resource` value published by /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource and must match the one sent to /authorize, otherwise `invalid_target`. For the token-exchange grant it is REQUIRED and must equal this API's own resource identifier exactly (never a front-end resource such as the MCP server), otherwise `invalid_target`.

subject_token.description: Token-exchange grant only. The front-end resource's access token being traded in. Must be a live, original (never itself exchanged) token minted for a resource this server issues tokens for, other than this API's own audience.

subject_token_type.description: Token-exchange grant only. Required; only `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token` is supported.

requested_token_type.description: Token-exchange grant only. Optional; when present it must agree with the only type this server issues.

issued_token_type.description: Present only for the token-exchange grant, per RFC 8693 §2.2.1.

expires_in.description: For the token-exchange grant, clamped to the subject token's own remaining lifetime as well as the exchanged-token TTL — never longer than either.

refresh_token.description: Present only when the `offline_access` scope was requested AND consented on the authorization_code/refresh_token grants. Never present for the token-exchange grant. Without it a client must send the user through the authorization flow again once the access token expires.

scope.description: The scope of the ACCESS token. `offline_access` is a request-time signal rather than a permission, so it never appears here even when it was requested.

id_token.description: A signed OIDC id_token (RS256). Present only when the openid scope was granted.

400.description: `invalid_grant` (bad, expired, replayed, or wrong-client authorization code; a `code_verifier` outside the RFC 7636 grammar of 43-128 unreserved characters; redirect_uri mismatch; a refresh token whose authorization no longer includes `offline_access`; for token-exchange, a `subject_token` that is unusable, itself an exchanged token, not visible to service clients, or expired), `invalid_target` (a `resource` this server does not issue tokens for, one disagreeing with the authorized value, or — for token-exchange — one other than this API's own resource identifier), `invalid_scope` (token-exchange only: the requested `scope` is not a subset of the subject token's own scopes), `invalid_request` (token-exchange only: an unsupported `subject_token_type`/`requested_token_type`), or `unsupported_grant_type`

401.description: `invalid_client` — unknown/disabled client or failed client authentication. The description never reveals whether client_id exists.

role_id.description: The template role ID associated with the signer.

id.description: The signer ID. The signer must already exist in the account.

verification_method.description: Verification method for this signer. If provided without notification_methods, the notification method is inferred. Defaults to Email. `DigitalCertificate` has the signer sign with their own ICP-Brasil certificate — it requires the Digital Certificate feature, the signer must have a CPF or CNPJ in `government_id` (a CPF requires that person's certificate; a CNPJ requires an e-CNPJ for that company), must be alone in its signing step, and is charged 2 credits per signer. Only applies to signers (not copy receivers).

notification_methods.description: Notification method codes for this signer. If provided without verification_method, the verification method is inferred. Defaults to Email. Only one method allowed per signer.

step.description: Positive integer that controls signing order. Signers sharing the same step sign in parallel; a step activates only after every signer in the previous step has signed. tags.description:
Steps to quickly start using the API. By the end you'll be able to create a document and invite signers.

### 1. Create a user account

During development, create a user account in the **sandbox** (https://app-sandbox.assinafy.com.br). For integrations using an API key, create a *separate* user account (e.g. *My App*) so you can grant it only the access it needs. Use the production app (https://app.assinafy.com.br) once you go live.

### 2. Set up credentials

Generate an **API key** from the *My Account → API* page in the Assinafy app, and note your **workspace account ID** from *My Account → Workspaces*. Use the API key only from a back-end system — never store it in client-side code.

For sandbox plan/credit purchases, use the test card `5510 3647 0363 3414`.

### 3. Upload a document

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts/{account_id}/documents" \
  -H 'X-Api-Key: {api_key}' \
  -F 'file=@/tmp/document.pdf'
```

Save the returned document `id` for the next steps.

### 4. Create signers

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts/{account_id}/signers" \
  -H 'X-Api-Key: {api_key}' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "full_name": "John Dove", "email": "john@example.com" }'
```

Save each signer `id`.

### 5. Request signatures

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/documents/{document_id}/assignments" \
  -H 'X-Api-Key: {api_key}' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "method": "virtual", "signers": [{ "id": "{signer_id}" }] }'
```

The `virtual` method requires no input from the signer. To collect input fields, use the `collect` method — see the Assignment section.

tags.name: SDKs & Tools
tags.description:
Official client libraries, a command-line tool, an MCP server and an n8n node — all built against the same OpenAPI document that generates this reference. Source for everything lives at [github.com/assinafy](https://github.com/assinafy).

Every SDK exposes the same operations and reads the same credentials:

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `ASSINAFY_API_KEY` | API key, sent as the `X-Api-Key` header. Create it from *My Account → API*. |
| `ASSINAFY_ACCOUNT_ID` | Workspace account id, from *My Account → Workspaces*. |
| `ASSINAFY_BASE_URL` | `https://sandbox.assinafy.com.br/v1` while developing, `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1` in production. |

An API key is a long-lived secret with full workspace access. Use it only from a back-end system — never in a browser bundle or a shipped mobile app.

## Server-side SDKs

| Language | Package | Install | Source |
|----------|---------|---------|--------|
| TypeScript / Node | `@assinafy/sdk` | `npm install @assinafy/sdk` | [typescript-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/typescript-sdk) |
| Python | `assinafy` | `pip install assinafy` | [python-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/python-sdk) |
| Ruby | `assinafy` | `gem "assinafy"` | [ruby-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/ruby-sdk) |
| Go | `github.com/assinafy/golang-sdk` | `go get github.com/assinafy/golang-sdk` | [golang-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/golang-sdk) |
| Rust | `assinafy` | `cargo add assinafy` | [rust-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/rust-sdk) |
| C# / .NET | `Assinafy.Sdk` | `dotnet add package Assinafy.Sdk` | [csharp-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/csharp-sdk) |
| Java | `com.assinafy:assinafy-sdk` | GitHub Packages — see below | [java-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/java-sdk) |
| PHP | `assinafy/php-sdk` | `composer require assinafy/php-sdk` | [php-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/php-sdk) |

Runtime floors are current-generation: Node 22+, Python 3.10+, Ruby 3.2+, Go 1.26+, Rust 1.86+, .NET 8+, JDK 25, PHP 8.2+.

### Which Java package?

Two Java artifacts exist and they are close to identical — both ship `com.assinafy.sdk.AssinafyClient` covering the same operations. Use **java-sdk** (`com.assinafy:assinafy-sdk`) for new integrations. **webforms-java-client** (`com.assinafy:webforms-java-client-sdk`, [source](https://github.com/assinafy/webforms-java-client)) is the same client with an older setter-style options builder, kept for integrations already on it; despite the name it carries no webforms-specific API.

Neither is published to Maven Central. Both resolve from GitHub Packages at `https://maven.pkg.github.com/assinafy/{repository}`, which requires a GitHub personal access token with `read:packages` even for public artifacts.

### Which TypeScript package?

`@assinafy/sdk` is the general-purpose REST client and the right default. [`@assinafy/chat-sdk`](https://github.com/assinafy/chat-sdk) bundles that same client *plus* chat orchestration, renderable cards, adapter and state contracts, and provider-neutral AI tool definitions — reach for it only when you are building a conversational signing experience.

## Mobile SDKs

| Platform | Install | Source |
|----------|---------|--------|
| iOS / macOS | SwiftPM — add the package URL `https://github.com/assinafy/mobile-ios-sdk.git` and pin *Up to Next Major* from the current release | [mobile-ios-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/mobile-ios-sdk) |
| Android | Gradle — `implementation("com.assinafy:assinafy-android-sdk:{version}")`, resolved from GitHub Packages (token required) | [mobile-android-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/mobile-android-sdk) |

Both are released on GitHub Releases; take the current version from the *Releases* page of the repository rather than a number quoted here.

**Never embed an account API key in a distributed app.** A key extracted from an app bundle grants full access to the workspace. Have the app authenticate against your own back end and receive a short-lived access token, or keep account operations server-side entirely.

## Command line

[`@assinafy/cli`](https://github.com/assinafy/assinafy-cli) exposes the API as a terminal tool: readable tables by default, `--json` for scripting, and named profiles so sandbox and production credentials stay apart.

```shell
npm install -g @assinafy/cli
assinafy login
assinafy send contract.pdf --signer "Ana Lima <ana@example.com>" --message "Please sign this contract"
```

## MCP server

A Model Context Protocol server that lets an AI assistant work with documents in your workspace. It is **hosted by Assinafy — there is nothing to install or deploy**.

| | |
|---|---|
| Endpoint | `POST https://mcp.assinafy.com.br/mcp` |
| Transport | Streamable HTTP (remote) |
| Authentication | OAuth 2.0 only — API keys are not accepted |

Add it to your MCP client as a **remote HTTP** server; there is no local command to run. On first use the client opens a browser window where you sign in to Assinafy, choose a workspace and approve the requested permissions. You do not create an OAuth application or enter a client ID, client secret, API key or workspace header — the client identifies itself with a Client ID Metadata Document. For example, in Claude Code:

```shell
claude mcp add --transport http assinafy https://mcp.assinafy.com.br/mcp
claude mcp login assinafy
```

The default scopes requested are `account:read`, `documents:read`, `documents:write`, `templates:read` and `templates:write`, plus `offline_access` when the client wants a refresh token. Setup for other clients (VS Code, Codex and more) is in the [MCP server documentation](https://github.com/assinafy/mcp-server/blob/main/README.en.md).

Eleven tools are exposed:

- **Documents** — `assinafy_find_documents`, `assinafy_prepare_document`, `assinafy_download_document`, `assinafy_verify_document`, `assinafy_delete_document`
- **Signature requests** — `assinafy_request_signatures`, `assinafy_follow_up_assignment`, `assinafy_check_fields`
- **Signers** — `assinafy_find_signers`, `assinafy_save_signer`
- **Templates** — `assinafy_find_templates`

Template creation, page-layout editing, role configuration and signer-side operations (signing, verification codes, term acceptance) are deliberately not exposed to assistants. Use the REST API for those.

## n8n

[`@assinafy/n8n-nodes-assinafy`](https://github.com/assinafy/n8n-nodes-assinafy) ships three pieces: an **Assinafy** action node covering assignments, documents, fields, signers, tags, templates, webhooks and workspaces; an **Assinafy Trigger** webhook node; and a shared **Assinafy API** credential holding the API key, the account id and the environment (production, sandbox or a custom base URL).

On self-hosted n8n, open **Settings → Community Nodes** and enter `@assinafy/n8n-nodes-assinafy`, or install it in the n8n container directly:

```shell
npm install @assinafy/n8n-nodes-assinafy
```

The Trigger node derives its webhook URL authentication from the credential and can additionally verify an HMAC-SHA256 payload signature, so a subscription created from n8n needs no extra webhook setup on the Assinafy side. Availability in n8n Cloud follows n8n's own community-node review.

## In practice

```javascript
import { AssinafyClient } from '@assinafy/sdk';

const client = new AssinafyClient({
  apiKey: process.env.ASSINAFY_API_KEY,
  accountId: process.env.ASSINAFY_ACCOUNT_ID,
});

const result = await client.uploadAndRequestSignatures({
  source: { filePath: './contract.pdf' },
  signers: [{ name: 'John Dove', email: 'john@example.com' }],
  message: 'Please sign this contract',
});

console.log(result.document.id);
```

```python
import os
from assinafy import AssinafyClient

with AssinafyClient(
    api_key=os.environ['ASSINAFY_API_KEY'],
    account_id=os.environ['ASSINAFY_ACCOUNT_ID'],
) as client:
    result = client.upload_and_request_signatures(
        source={'file_path': './contract.pdf'},
        signers=[{'full_name': 'John Dove', 'email': 'john@example.com'}],
        message='Please sign this contract',
    )
    print(result['document']['id'])
```

tags.name: OpenAPI & API Clients
tags.description:
This reference is generated from a single OpenAPI 3.0 document. You can download that document and load it into any OpenAPI-aware tool — Postman, Insomnia, a code generator, or your editor.

## Download the spec

The document is served at `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json` and always describes what is currently deployed:

```shell
curl -o assinafy-openapi.json "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json"
```


## Postman

There are two ways in.

**Fork the ready-made collection.** Open the [Assinafy Postman collection](https://www.postman.com/devassinafy/dev-assinafy-s-workspace/collection/tqqxlsd/assinafy-api-collection), select the Assinafy Collection, then **Fork** it into your own workspace.

**Or import the spec yourself:**

1. **Import → Link**, paste `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json` and confirm. Postman creates a request for every operation, grouped by section.
2. On the new collection, open **Authorization**, choose **API Key**, set *Key* to `X-Api-Key`, *Value* to `{{api_key}}` and *Add to* **Header**. Every request inherits it.
3. Create an **environment** holding `base_url` (`https://sandbox.assinafy.com.br/v1` while developing) and `api_key`. Keep the key in the environment rather than the collection so it does not travel with an exported or shared collection.

## Insomnia

1. **Create → Import → From URL**, paste `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json`.
2. Open **Manage Environments** on the imported collection and add:

```json
{
  "base_url": "https://sandbox.assinafy.com.br/v1",
  "api_key": "your-api-key"
}
```

3. On the collection's **Headers** tab add `X-Api-Key` with value `{{ _.api_key }}` so every request inherits it.

Switching between sandbox and production is then a matter of selecting a different environment.

## Generate your own client

The document works with the usual generators:

```shell
npx @openapitools/openapi-generator-cli generate \
  -i https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json \
  -g python \
  -o ./assinafy-client
```

Worth weighing first: the official SDKs listed under *SDKs & Tools* already unwrap the `{ status, message, data }` envelope, surface the `X-Pagination-*` response headers as pagination objects, and handle multipart document upload. A generated client hands you the raw envelope on every call and leaves that work to you.

tags.name: Authentication
tags.description:
Authentication can be done in three ways:

- API key in the `X-Api-Key` header: `X-Api-Key: {api-key}`
- Access token in the `Authorization` header: `Authorization: Bearer {access-token}`
- Access token as a URL parameter: `?access-token={access-token}`

The **recommended** method is an API key, which you create from the settings page in the Assinafy app. An access token is obtained through login with email and password; it is a JWT that usually expires in one hour.

Building an application that **other people** connect to their own workspace? Don't ask for their API key: use OAuth, which gives your app a token limited to what the user approved. See **OAuth Integration Guide**.

tags.name: OAuth Integration Guide
tags.description:
Build an application that **other people connect to their own Assinafy workspace**, without ever handling their password or API key. The user approves your app once; you receive tokens limited to the permissions they approved and to one workspace. Standard OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect libraries work unchanged.

### Do you need OAuth?

| | API key | OAuth |
|---|---|---|
| Acts on | **Your own** workspace | **Someone else's** workspace, with their permission |
| Can do | Everything your account can do | Only what the user approved |
| The user can switch it off | No | Yes, at any time |
| Choose it when | You automate your own account | You build an app that other people connect |

Automating your own workspace? Keep using your API key; nothing in this guide applies.

### How it works

1. Your app sends the user's browser to the authorization server, `https://auth.assinafy.com.br`.
2. The user signs in, picks **one** workspace and approves your app.
3. The browser comes back to your site with a one-time code.
4. Your server exchanges the code for tokens at `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/token`.
5. Your server calls this API with `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>`.

Two hosts on purpose: the browser page lives on the authorization server, and everything your code calls lives on this API.

### Create your application

You must be an **owner** of the workspace that will own the application, and the workspace's plan must include OAuth applications. In the Assinafy app (https://app.assinafy.com.br), open **Settings → OAuth applications → New application**.

| Field | What to put |
|---|---|
| Name | What users see on the approval screen |
| Description | One sentence on what the app does with their documents |
| Logo URL | Optional, an `https://` image |
| Redirect URIs | Where users return after approving, e.g. `https://myapp.com/oauth/callback`. Must be `https://`, without `#`, and is matched **exactly**: `…/callback` and `…/callback/` are different. Add one per environment you run. For local development use an https tunnel; `http://localhost` is not accepted |
| Permissions | The **most** your app will ever request. You can ask for less at connect time, never more |
| Type | **Confidential** if your code runs on a server you control; **Public** if it runs on the user's device and cannot keep a secret. Cannot be changed later |

You get a `client_id` (public) and, for Confidential apps, a `client_secret`.

> **The secret is shown once.** Store it in your server's secret storage straight away. If it is lost, rotate it: the old secret stops working immediately, so deploy the new one at once. Deleting the application disconnects every user immediately.

Building one product that **many different Assinafy customers** will connect? Talk to us first: we can register it as a verified application owned by no single workspace, with one `client_id` for every customer.

### Discovery

Most OAuth libraries only need the issuer, `https://auth.assinafy.com.br`, and read the rest from its metadata document. If you configure URLs by hand, copy them from there:

```shell
curl "https://auth.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server"
```

```json
{
  "issuer": "https://auth.assinafy.com.br",
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://auth.assinafy.com.br/oauth/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/token",
  "revocation_endpoint": "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/revoke",
  "userinfo_endpoint": "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/userinfo",
  "jwks_uri": "https://auth.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/jwks.json",
  "response_types_supported": ["code"],
  "grant_types_supported": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_post", "none"]
}
```

The metadata and key documents are served **only** by the authorization server. This API serves its own protected-resource metadata at `https://api.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`.

### Connect a user

#### 1. Create a PKCE pair and a state

PKCE is required for **every** application, Confidential ones included. Create a new pair for each connection attempt:

```js
import crypto from 'node:crypto';

const b64url = (buf) => buf.toString('base64url');

const codeVerifier  = b64url(crypto.randomBytes(32));
const codeChallenge = b64url(crypto.createHash('sha256').update(codeVerifier).digest());
const state         = b64url(crypto.randomBytes(16));

// Keep codeVerifier and state in the user's session: step 3 and 4 need them.
```

The verifier must be 43 to 128 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~`.

#### 2. Send the browser to the authorization server

Use a full page navigation (a link or a redirect), not an AJAX call. Shown unencoded for readability; URL-encode every value:

```
https://auth.assinafy.com.br/oauth/authorize
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID
  &redirect_uri=https://myapp.com/oauth/callback
  &scope=documents:read documents:write offline_access
  &state=STATE
  &code_challenge=CODE_CHALLENGE
  &code_challenge_method=S256
  &resource=https://api.assinafy.com.br
```

| Parameter | Notes |
|---|---|
| `redirect_uri` | One of your registered URIs, character for character |
| `scope` | Space-separated, within what the application is registered for |
| `state` | Random per attempt; your CSRF protection |
| `code_challenge_method` | Only `S256` |
| `resource` | `https://api.assinafy.com.br`, naming the API the token is for. Recommended |
| `nonce` | Optional, echoed in the `id_token` when you request `openid` |

If the `client_id` or `redirect_uri` is wrong, the user is **not** sent back to you: the authorization server shows an error on its own page, because redirecting to an unverified address would be unsafe. Users reporting that they are stuck on an Assinafy error page usually means one of those two values is wrong.

#### 3. Handle the return

Approved:

```
https://myapp.com/oauth/callback?code=…&state=…&iss=https://auth.assinafy.com.br
```

Declined or invalid:

```
https://myapp.com/oauth/callback?error=access_denied&error_description=…&state=…&iss=https://auth.assinafy.com.br
```

Before anything else, check that `state` equals what you stored and that `iss` equals `https://auth.assinafy.com.br`. If either differs, stop: the response is not yours.

#### 4. Exchange the code for tokens

From your server. The code is single-use and expires **60 seconds** after approval.

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/token" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d code=THE_CODE \
  -d redirect_uri=https://myapp.com/oauth/callback \
  -d client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d code_verifier=THE_CODE_VERIFIER \
  -d resource=https://api.assinafy.com.br
```

Public applications send the same request without `client_secret`.

```json
{
  "access_token": "…",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "scope": "documents:read documents:write offline_access",
  "refresh_token": "…",
  "id_token": "…"
}
```

- `refresh_token` is present only when you requested `offline_access`; `id_token` only when you requested `openid`.
- `scope` is what you **actually** received. Read it instead of assuming.
- OAuth token responses are plain JSON objects, not wrapped in the `{ status, message, data }` envelope the rest of this API uses.

#### 5. Find the workspace, then call the API

A token belongs to the one workspace the user picked. With an OAuth token, the workspace list returns exactly that workspace:

```shell
curl "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts" \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN'
```

Store `data[0].id` next to the tokens, then call the API:

```shell
curl "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts/WORKSPACE_ID/documents" \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN'
```

Always send the token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. A token sent as `X-Api-Key` or in the query string is refused.

### Permissions (scopes)

| Scope | Lets your app |
|---|---|
| `documents:read` | Read documents, their signers, assignments and activity, the WhatsApp notifications sent for an assignment, and webhook event types and delivery history |
| `documents:write` | Create documents and send them for signature |
| `templates:read` | Read templates |
| `templates:write` | Create and change templates |
| `account:read` | Read the workspace's profile, theme and logo, and read the workspace's webhook subscription |
| `webhooks:write` | Change where and which webhook events are delivered, and deactivate the webhook subscription |
| `openid` | Receive an `id_token` identifying the user |
| `profile` | Read the user's name |
| `email` | Read the user's email and whether it is verified |
| `offline_access` | Receive a refresh token, to keep working while the user is away |

- Request the minimum. Every permission is another line the user reads before deciding.
- `documents:write` can spend the workspace's notification credits, since sending for signature notifies signers.
- The user approves everything you requested, or nothing. If a feature needs more later, run the flow again requesting the larger set.
- Billing and subscriptions, workspace membership, credentials and administration are **never** available to an OAuth token, whatever its scopes.

Calling an endpoint without the scope it requires returns `403` with a challenge naming the missing scope:

```
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="documents:write", resource_metadata="https://api.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"
```

Treat it as a prompt to reconnect with that scope added, not as a request to retry. A `403` without this header has another cause: a different workspace, the user's own role, or an area OAuth tokens can never reach.

### Resource indicators

`resource` (RFC 8707) names **which service** a token is for. Omit it and you get a token for
this API — that is what every direct integration wants, and nothing about it has changed.

Assinafy also runs a separate MCP server, which is its own protected resource. A token minted
for it authenticates against *that* server and is refused here, and the reverse is also true.
If you are calling this API directly, send `https://api.assinafy.com.br` or omit the parameter.

A refresh may repeat the original `resource` but never change it; a different value is
rejected with `invalid_target`.

> **Operator note.** The confidential client backing Assinafy's own MCP server is an
> **internal-service client** (`is_internal_service`), provisioned outside this
> self-serve flow. It has no `redirect_uris` and cannot pass through the ordinary
> secret-rotation endpoint — that write requires `redirect_uris` under the client's
> default validation scenario, which an internal-service client deliberately has none
> of. If its secret leaks, the recovery path is **disable the client and provision a
> new one**, then reconfigure the MCP server with the new credentials — not "rotate the
> secret."

### One connection, one workspace

The integration mistake we see most often. A token works only for the workspace the user chose; calling any other workspace returns `403`, even one the same user belongs to. If your customer uses several workspaces, connect each one separately and keep tokens per workspace.

### Refresh tokens

Access tokens last **1 hour**. With `offline_access`, renew them without the user:

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/token" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token \
  -d refresh_token=CURRENT_REFRESH_TOKEN \
  -d client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
```

Every refresh returns a **new** refresh token and retires the old one.

> **Using an old refresh token disconnects the user.** A reused refresh token cannot be told apart from a stolen one being replayed, so it ends the whole connection: every token stops working and the user must connect again.
>
> 1. Save the new refresh token before doing anything else with the response.
> 2. Treat a timeout as "maybe it worked": re-read your saved token before retrying, never retry blindly with the old one.
> 3. Refresh one at a time per connection.

- A refresh token is valid for **30 days**, and every refresh returns a new one with a fresh 30 days. A connection only expires if your app goes 30 days without refreshing; after that, the user has to reconnect.
- If the user approves your app again with different permissions, the previous tokens stop working immediately.

### Disconnecting

When a user disconnects in your product, revoke the token instead of only deleting it. The endpoint always answers `200`:

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/revoke" \
  -d token=THE_REFRESH_OR_ACCESS_TOKEN \
  -d client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
```

Users can also revoke your app themselves under **Connected apps** in their Assinafy profile. Deleting or disabling your application has the same effect. In every case your tokens stop working at once: handle the `401` by asking the user to connect again.

> **Revoking a token requires the `client_id` that owns it.** `/oauth/revoke` only revokes a token issued to the client authenticating the call. This matters for an RFC 8693 exchanged token specifically: it carries the *original* (front-end resource) client's id, not the service client that exchanged it — so a back-channel service client can never revoke a token it derived, and the call still answers `200` per RFC 7009's always-succeed contract, giving no indication that nothing happened. That derived token is inherently short-lived (bounded by the exchanged-token TTL), so it ages out on its own; do not build a cleanup call expecting revoke to work on it.

### Verification and limits

- New applications are **unverified**: the approval screen warns that Assinafy has not reviewed the app, and it can be connected to at most **25 workspaces**. Before launching beyond a pilot, ask us to verify it, telling us what the app does and why it needs each permission.
- The authorize and token endpoints accept **50 requests per minute per IP**. Normal traffic stays far below that; hitting it usually means a refresh loop.
- Applications are created in the Assinafy app, not through an API.

### Errors

On your redirect URI (`?error=…`):

| `error` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `access_denied` | The user declined |
| `invalid_scope` | A scope your application is not registered for, or none |
| `invalid_request` | Missing or malformed PKCE parameters |
| `unsupported_response_type` | Anything other than `response_type=code` |
| `invalid_target` | A `resource` other than `https://api.assinafy.com.br` |

From the token endpoint (`{ "error": "…", "error_description": "…" }`):

| `error` | Usual causes |
|---|---|
| `invalid_grant` | Code expired or already used, wrong `code_verifier` or `redirect_uri`; refresh token already used or expired, or the user reconnected with different permissions |
| `invalid_client` | Wrong `client_id` or secret, or the application is disabled |
| `invalid_target` | `resource` does not match what was authorized |
| `unsupported_grant_type` | Only `authorization_code` and `refresh_token` exist |

From API calls:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `401` | Token expired, revoked, or not sent as `Bearer`. Refresh; if that fails, ask the user to reconnect |
| `403` with `insufficient_scope` | Missing permission. Reconnect requesting the scope in `WWW-Authenticate` |
| `403` otherwise | Another workspace, or an area OAuth tokens cannot reach |
| `429` | Too many requests. Back off and retry later |

### Signing users in (OpenID Connect)

Request `openid`, plus `profile` and/or `email`, to receive an `id_token`: a signed JWT saying who approved. Validate it with any OpenID Connect library:

- signature `RS256`, keys at `https://auth.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/jwks.json` (match the `kid`);
- `iss` equals `https://auth.assinafy.com.br`;
- `aud` equals your `client_id`;
- `exp` is in the future, and `nonce` matches the one you sent, if any.

`sub` is the user's stable identifier. For their name and email, call **OpenID Connect userinfo** (`GET https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/userinfo`).

### AI assistants

Claude, Claude Code and ChatGPT connect to Assinafy on their own through their connector settings. Your users do not need you to build or register anything for them.

### Before you go live

- A new PKCE verifier and `state` for every connection attempt
- `state` and `iss` checked on your redirect URI
- `client_secret` only on your server, never in a mobile app, browser code or a repository
- The new refresh token saved before use, and one refresh at a time per connection
- `401` handled: refresh, and if that fails, ask the user to reconnect
- The workspace id stored per connection, and the returned `scope` read
- Every production redirect URI registered, `https://` and exact
- Only the permissions you need
- Tokens revoked when a user disconnects
- Verification requested

tags.name: Verification & Notification Methods
tags.description:
When you create an assignment, each signer can be configured with a **verification method** (how the signer proves their identity before signing) and a **notification method** (how the signer is told a signature is being requested). Exactly one notification method is allowed per signer; `notification_methods` is an array for historical reasons, and sending more than one entry returns `400`. These are set per signer via `signers[].verification_method` and `signers[].notification_methods` on the **Create assignment** endpoint.

Verification and notification are **coupled** — you may send one, both or neither, and the missing side is inferred. If neither is sent, both default to `Email`.

### Verification methods

| Code | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `Email` | The signer receives a verification code by email that must be entered before signing. |
| `Whatsapp` | The signer receives a verification code over WhatsApp that must be entered before signing. Requires the WhatsApp notification channel — the two always travel together. |
| `DigitalCertificate` | The signer signs with their own ICP-Brasil digital certificate (A1/A3) from their device using the Web PKI browser extension, producing a qualified PAdES signature on the document. |

| Code | Requirements | Cost per signer (verification + its notification) |
|------|--------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `Email` | Signer must have an email address. | 0 credits (the Email notification) |
| `Whatsapp` | Signer must have a `whatsapp_phone_number`; available only on paid subscriptions. | 0.45 credits (the WhatsApp notification, which this method requires) |
| `DigitalCertificate` | Account must have the **Digital Certificate** feature (Standard and Pro plans). Signer must have a CPF in `government_id`. Each digital-certificate signer must be **alone in its signing step**. | 2 credits + its notification |

> **How verification is priced.** No verification method carries a price of its own — you are billed for the **notification** it is paired with (plus, for `DigitalCertificate`, the signature itself). Because verification and notification are coupled, choosing `Whatsapp` verification also chooses the WhatsApp notification, so a WhatsApp-verified signer costs 0.45 credits against 0 credits for an email-verified one. The column above is that combined per-signer cost, which is what the **Estimate assignment cost** endpoint returns.

> **Digital Certificate cost.** Unlike the other verification methods (whose only cost is the notification), the digital-certificate signature itself is charged **2 credits per digital-certificate signer**, on top of the notification cost. The charge is applied when the assignment is created, and appears in the **Estimate assignment cost** breakdown under the `SignatureDigitalCertificate` code.

### Notification methods

The notification method is what delivers the signing invitation to the signer. Each notification has a credit cost charged when the assignment is created (and again when a notification is resent).

| Code | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `Email` | Sends an email invitation with a link to sign the document. |
| `Whatsapp` | Sends a WhatsApp message with a link to sign the document. |

| Code | Requirements | Cost (per signer) |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| `Email` | Signer must have an email address. | 0 credits |
| `Whatsapp` | Signer must have a `whatsapp_phone_number`; available only on paid subscriptions. | 0.45 credits |

### Coupling rules

Only matching combinations are allowed; an invalid pairing returns `400 Bad Request`.

| Verification method | Allowed notification methods |
|---------------------|------------------------------|
| `Email` | `Email` |
| `Whatsapp` | `Whatsapp` |
| `DigitalCertificate` | `Email` or `Whatsapp` |

Exactly one notification method is allowed per signer — `notification_methods` takes a single-element array, and a second entry is rejected with `400` before the pairing above is even checked.

### Default behavior (inference)

- **Neither specified** — both default to `Email`.
- **Only `verification_method`** — `notification_methods` is inferred from it (e.g. `Whatsapp` verification → `Whatsapp` notification, and with it that channel's cost).
- **Only `notification_methods`** — `verification_method` is inferred from it.
- **Both specified** — used as-is, subject to the coupling rules above.

### Costs

Notification cost is charged **per signer**, on top of the document cost. For example:

- 2 signers notified by email = 0 credits
- 2 signers notified by WhatsApp = 0.9 credits

Verification follows the same arithmetic, because it is the notification that is billed: 2 signers **verified** by WhatsApp are necessarily notified by WhatsApp, and therefore also cost 0.9 credits.

Use the **Estimate assignment cost** endpoint to preview the exact total (documents + notifications) before creating an assignment.

### Notification timing and sequential signing

By default every signer is notified as soon as the assignment is created. When you set `signers[].step` to define a signing order, each signer's notification is held until their step is activated: step 1 is notified at creation, and a later step is notified only after every signer in the previous step has finished.

tags.name: Webhook Payloads
tags.description:
This section documents the HTTP request your endpoint receives whenever a subscribed event is triggered, and the shape of the JSON body sent for each event type.

### Delivery contract

When an event occurs, we send an HTTP `POST` request to the endpoint configured in your webhook subscription.

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Method | `POST` |
| Content-Type | `application/json` |
| Connection header | `close` |
| Success criteria | Any `2xx` response |
| Attempts | Up to 2 per event (initial attempt + 1 retry) |
| Retry wait | 3 seconds between attempts |
| Circuit breaker | After 10 consecutive failed events, delivery is paused and only ~5% of events are probed until one succeeds. Use the **Retry webhook delivery** endpoint to force redelivery. |
| Response capture | We store the first 2000 characters of your response body for debugging (see **List webhook deliveries**). |

Your endpoint must respond within a reasonable time and return a `2xx` status. Non-`2xx` responses, connection errors and timeouts are all treated as failed deliveries and count toward the circuit breaker.

### Common envelope

Every webhook body shares the same top-level structure:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `id` | integer | Internal activity ID that produced this event. Useful for deduplication on your side. |
| `event` | string | Event type identifier. See the catalog below and the **List webhook event types** endpoint. |
| `message` | string \\| null | Human-readable message describing the event. May contain token placeholders. Can be `null`. |
| `payload` | object \\| null | Event-specific parameters. Keys vary per event — see the catalog. Can be `null`. |
| `origin` | object \\| null | Where the action was triggered from, when available: `{ ip, user-agent }`. |
| `created_at` | integer | Unix timestamp (seconds) when the event was recorded. |
| `subject` | object | The entity that performed the action. Polymorphic — see below. |
| `object` | object | The entity the action was performed on. Polymorphic — see below. |
| `account_id` | string | The ID of the account that owns this event. Always present. |

### About `subject` and `object`

Both are **polymorphic**: their shape depends on which entity they represent. We always add a `type` property with the entity class name, one of `User`, `Signer`, `Account`, `Document`, or `Template`. The remaining properties match the same fields the REST API returns for that resource. The `object` is serialized with its extra relationships expanded (e.g. a `Document` includes `assignment` and `pages`); the `subject` carries its base fields only. Whenever `subject` or `object` is an `Account`, the `integration` property (which includes dispatch history) is removed before sending.

For `document_ready`, `document_processing_failed` and `template_processing_failed`, the `subject` is the `Account` itself — these events are emitted by the system when processing finishes, not by a particular user.

### Event catalog

| Event | Subject | Object | `payload` keys | Description |
|-------|---------|--------|----------------|-------------|
| `document_uploaded` | User | Document | — | The user uploaded a new document. |
| `document_metadata_ready` | User | Document | — | The document was normalized to PDF and its pages are available. |
| `document_prepared` | User | Document | — | The user prepared a document (fields assigned to signers). |
| `assignment_created` | User | Document | `user_name`, `user_email`, `user_telephone` | The user created an assignment for the document. Includes a snapshot of the creator profile. |
| `document_ready` | Account | Document | — | The last signer signed the document; status is now `ready`. |
| `document_processing_failed` | Account | Document | `error_message` | The document could not be processed. |
| `signature_requested` | User | Document | `signer_email` / `signer_full_name` / `signer_whatsapp_phone_number` (depending on notification method) | The user requested a signer to sign the document. |
| `signer_created` | User | Signer | `signer_full_name` | The user created a new signer. |
| `signer_email_verified` | Signer | Document | `signer_email` | The signer's email was verified through a code linked to the document. |
| `signer_whatsapp_verified` | Signer | Document | `signer_whatsapp_phone_number` | The signer's WhatsApp number was verified through a code linked to the document. |
| `signer_data_confirmed` | Signer | Document | `signer_email` | The signer confirmed their data before signing. |
| `signer_viewed_document` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name` | The signer opened the document for the first time. |
| `signer_signed_document` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name` | The signer signed the document. |
| `signer_rejected_document` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name` | The signer refused to sign the document. |
| `user_rejected_document` | User | Document | `user_name` | The document was cancelled by a user of the account. |
| `template_created` | User | Template | — | The user created a new template. |
| `template_processed` | User | Template | — | A template's metadata was processed and is ready for use. |
| `template_processing_failed` | Account | Template | `error_message` | A template could not be processed. |

`assignment_created` and `document_metadata_ready` have no guaranteed ordering: under the virtual pre-metadata flow, `assignment_created` may fire before `document_metadata_ready`. Treat any unknown field as a forward-compatible addition.
